title: Testing a choice-based anime story scene made with AI — looking for feedback
author: Fearless_Shift7108
selftext:
I’m testing an early AI-native game prototype where the player watches a short anime-style story scene, gets a choice in the middle, and then the story continues based on what they pick.

It’s not meant to be just an AI video or animation clip. The idea is closer to a small playable visual novel-style scene, with characters, dialogue, choices, and follow-up story moments.

I’m curious how people here think about this kind of AI-assisted game format. Does the choice moment make it feel more like an actual game, or would it need clearer consequences, stronger branching, or more player control to feel meaningful?

replies.author: Statcat2017
replies.body: But the entire genre failed because it is just "watch a video and click once". Once the tech was no longer impressive the genre died overnight.

replies.author: Fearless_Shift7108
replies.body:
Yeah, that’s exactly the risk I’m worried about too. If it only stays as “watch a clip, click once, then watch another clip,” I agree it probably won’t hold up once the visual novelty wears off.

For this test, we’re mainly using the scene to explore the format, but the real challenge is building more actual gameplay around it — repeated meaningful choices, visible consequences, character/state changes, and reasons to replay instead of just passively watching branches.

So I think your point is fair: the generated video part can’t be the whole product. It has to support the gameplay loop, not replace it.

replies.author: Crimes_Optimal
replies.body:
I feel like what you're missing is that it isn't a consequence of not being creative enough within the genre, it's the *nature of* the genre. It's not a risk, it's what's going to happen. 

You can make it as responsive as you like, you can make as many small alterations as you want, you can go through player choice with a fine toothed comb and make every little decision matter, but from the player's point of view, they will still be clicking once and then watching a video. You look back at the history of these kinds of games, from those 90s FMV games to more modern stuff like Telltale or Dispatch, the first playthrough always feels like it's reacting perfectly to your decisions, and the seams only show on later playthroughs. The obvious problem, of course, is that the vast majority of players will only play it once, if that. What sets your game apart from any given AI-generated story you see a million of scrolling through YouTube or Facebook besides that?

You say it has to support the gameplay loop and not replace it, but what does that look like? What is the rest of your gameplay loop that makes it no longer an interactive movie? That's something you need to design before you start making *anything*.

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body: Big choice for you to make: is the AI writing the story as you go, or do you pre write everything and then connect it together?

replies.author: Fearless_Shift7108
replies.body:
That’s exactly one of the biggest design choices we’re thinking about.

Right now, we’re leaning more toward a hybrid approach rather than fully AI-written or fully pre-written. The idea is to have enough structure so the story doesn’t become random or incoherent, but still let AI help generate/extend scenes, choices, and follow-up moments based on what the player does.

Fully pre-writing everything gives more control, but it can feel less “AI-native.” Fully generating everything live is more flexible, but it can easily lose pacing, consistency, or narrative quality. So the challenge is finding the right balance between authored structure and AI-driven variation.

comments.author: monsterfurby
comments.body:
I suppose if the visuals were anime-styled, it would at least be less uncanny valley. That said, that style of gameplay always reminds me of terrible mobile ads, though I am a fan of choice-based games.

Part of that is that the way the choices are phrased is already heavily editorialized (aside from the typos). I would suggest you replace that with either direct dialogue lines / answers, or shorter bits. The problem with long explanatory lines like this is that they almost always telegraph what is going to happen and how the creator intends this to play out.

I would also suggest splitting scenes like this into smaller choices - some of which can be inconsequential, some of which pay into the result. Here, the two choices are very large, when there could be multiple points where the player has to decide whether to do one or the other by way of choosing the actual, concrete thing rather than a more indirect "directorial" choice.

replies.author: Fearless_Shift7108
replies.body:
This is really useful feedback, thank you.

I agree with the “terrible mobile ads” concern — that’s exactly something we want to avoid. The goal shouldn’t be “watch a scene and click the obvious option,” but to make the choices feel like something the player is actually doing.

Your point about the wording is especially helpful. Direct dialogue lines or shorter action-based choices probably would feel much better than long explanatory options, since long choices can make the result too predictable.

I also like the idea of breaking it into smaller choices instead of two huge directional decisions. More concrete micro-decisions could make the scene feel more playable and less like a scripted interactive movie. I’ll definitely keep this in mind while we iterate on the choice design.

replies.author: Fearless_Shift7108
replies.body:
Thank you, really appreciate the detailed feedback!

For the vocals/facial animation, most of the sync is handled through the generation pipeline rather than being manually animated frame by frame. We’re still experimenting with how to make the voices, expressions, and timing feel more natural, so I’m glad that part came across better than expected.

And yeah, great catch on the 0:28 moment. That scene transition is definitely jarring — the character positions should stay consistent instead of suddenly jumping into a wide semicircle. That’s something we need to improve with scene continuity, blocking, and shot-to-shot consistency.

Thanks again for pointing it out so specifically. This kind of feedback is really helpful while we’re still testing the format.

comments.author: DerekPaxton
comments.body:
The way you present the choice is everything.

You typically want the player to be able to focus on the scene, not take them out of it. Don't dim the entire background. Instead have the player looking at what you want them to look at and present the choices in a secondary area (typically below the scene, though to the left can work as well).

Also you may need sound design for choice selection to let the player know they are in interaction mode and they need to act. Something subtle like a small wave that builds in intensity the longer they sit in this mode.

There is also no reason for the A and B labels on the choices. Just offer the choices.

comments.author: verbalbacklash
comments.body: I tried my hand at writing Ai based choose your own adventure and here is the problem I see with this concept. Like many are saying it's and interactive movie circa 1995 all over again. What new game play or tech are you bringing to the table? Ai set dressing isn't enough to sell the story using the same model from back then. I don't want to poopoo your idea like others have if it a passion project and a story you want to tell that's one thing but its not a game. Boil it down to this, a game is "usually" something where you use a skill or intelligent choice to have your own experience. If you are trying to tell a dynamic story then don't call it a game , its still just a story and the audience for this is very low and currently very resistant to AI in general.  If its a game you have to give the player something to achieve  a goal that works with the players skills or intelligence there are few examples of successful games that don't have the player being the star and their choices for good or bad effecting the whole world. So would I suggest if your building a game you have to make the player front and center of the outcome. If not your telling a story which is fine but don't market it as a game and you will have a harder time because of all the push back on ai generated stories. Just my 2 cents but i hope it helps.
